mainTopic: When an owner gives up hope (יאוש) on a lost coin: coins dropped among a group or into sand, a finder's sins, and items found in a store, near a money changer, or inside produce
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא about a סלע seen falling from a group of people. If it fell from one of two, the finder must return it, because the owner can blame the other person and does not give up hope (יאוש). If it fell from one of three, the owner gives up hope, so the finder keeps it. רבא limits this case: if the coin is worth a פרוטה for each of the three, they may be partners who do not give up hope, so the finder must return it. A second version of רבא extends this even to two פרוטות. רבא then lists which commandments a finder breaks, depending on when he took the coin and what he meant to do with it. He also rules that coins that fall into sand belong to the finder, even if the owner is seen sifting for them. A new משנה follows. It decides who owns items found in a store or near a שולחני, based on where they lie, and it rules on coins found inside produce someone bought or received. The גמרא brings רבי אלעזר's ruling that even coins on the money changer's table go to the finder, tests it against the משנה, and has רבא explain its source. ריש לקיש then begins to limit the produce ruling, and his statement continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A coin that fell from one of two people must be returned
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that if a coin fell from one of two people, the finder must return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a coin fell from one of two people, the finder is obligated to return it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is in the middle of quoting a ברייתא about a coin seen falling from a group of people. Here it gives the first ruling: if it fell from one of two people, it must be returned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The finder does not know which of the two dropped the coin. Even so, he must return it. The next step explains why.

phrases.english: that fell from two people
phrases.notes: This picks up in the middle of the ברייתא: someone saw a סלע fall from one of two people.

phrases.english: he is obligated to return it.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A coin that fell from one of two people must be returned by the finder.

steps.title: Why the owner in the case of two does not give up hope
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the owner does not give up hope (יאוש), because he plans to blame the only other person who was with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? The one who dropped it does not give up hope. He thinks: no one else was with me except this man. I will grab him and say to him, 'You are the one who took it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the finder must return the coin. It answers that the owner has not given up hope of getting it back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An item only becomes the finder's once the owner gives up hope (יאוש). With only two people present, the owner assumes the other person took the coin and expects to get it back from him. So there is no יאוש, and the coin still belongs to the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Gives up hope (of recovering the item)
I will grab him (and confront him)

phrases.english: What is the reason?
The one from whom it fell does not give up hope.
He says to himself:

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּדֵי אִינִישׁ אַחֲרִינָא לָא הֲוָה בַּהֲדַאי
phrases.english: After all, no other person was with me
except this one.
phrases.notes: He does not know that a third person, the finder, picked it up.

phrases.english: I will grab him and say to him:
It is you who took it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? הָהוּא דִּנְפַל מִינֵּיהּ לָא מִיָּאַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the ruling in step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner does not give up hope, because he believes the other person took it and he can confront him.

steps.title: A coin that fell from one of three people need not be returned
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that if a coin fell from one of three people, the finder does not have to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it fell from one of three people, he is not obligated to return it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the second ruling. If the coin fell from one of three people, the finder may keep it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Adding just one more person changes the outcome. The next step explains why a third person makes the difference.

phrases.english: If it fell from one of three, he is not obligated to return it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the case of three with the case of two.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A coin that fell from one of three people may be kept by the finder.

steps.title: Why the owner in the case of three gives up hope
steps.stepSummary: With two other people present, the owner cannot blame either one with confidence, so he gives up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? The one who dropped it surely gives up hope. He thinks: two people were with me. If I grab this one, he will say 'I didn't take it,' and if I grab that one, he will say 'I didn't take it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the case of three. The owner gives up hope because he has no one specific to blame.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of the other two can deny taking the coin, and the owner cannot prove which one did. So he realizes he will never get it back, which is יאוש. Once there is יאוש, the finder may keep the coin.
steps.whatToRemember: Two people: the owner can blame the other one, so there is no יאוש and the finder must return it. Three people: the owner cannot pin it on anyone, so there is יאוש and the finder keeps it.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
The one from whom it fell certainly gives up hope.
He says to himself:
After all, two people were with me.
If I grab this one, he will say, 'I did not take it,'
and if I grab that one, he will say, 'I did not take it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? הָהוּא דִּנְפַל מִינֵּיהּ וַדַּאי מִיָּאַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the ruling in step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner gives up hope because each of the two others can deny taking it.

steps.title: רבא limits the case of three to small amounts
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the case of three applies only when the coin is worth less than a פרוטה per person. If each would get a פרוטה, the finder must return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: When you said that with three people he does not have to return it, we said this only when the coin is not worth a פרוטה for each one. But if it is worth a פרוטה for each one, he must return it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a limit to the ruling about three people. It only applies when the coin is too small to give each of them a פרוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Returning a lost item is required only if it is worth at least a פרוטה. רבא considers that the coin might belong to all three together. If each one's share is at least a פרוטה, the finder must return it.

keyTerms.meaning: Worth a פרוטה, the smallest amount that counts as money in הלכה

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not arguing with the ברייתא. He is narrowing the case of three to coins too small to give each person a פרוטה.

phrases.english: Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי דְּאָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לְהַחְזִיר –
phrases.english: That which you said, that with three he is not obligated to return it,
we said this only

phrases.aramaic: דְּלֵית בֵּיהּ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה לְכׇל חַד וְחַד,
phrases.english: where it is not worth a peruta for each and every one,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אִית בֵּיהּ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה לְכׇל חַד וְחַד –
phrases.english: but if it is worth a peruta for each and every one,
he is obligated to return it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הַאי דְּאָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלֹשָׁה אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לְהַחְזִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling about three people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the case of three, the finder must return the coin if it is worth at least a פרוטה per person.

steps.title: רבא's reason: they may be partners
steps.stepSummary: Perhaps the three are partners who own the coin together, so none of them gives up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Say they are partners, and they do not give up hope.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבא's ruling. Maybe the three people own the coin together, and partners do not give up hope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If they are partners, the coin was not lost by just one of them. Each partner assumes one of the others picked it up for the group, so none of them gives up hope. Since each one's share is at least a פרוטה, every one of them has a real loss that must be returned.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Say that they are partners, and they do not give up hope.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? אֵימוֹר שׁוּתָּפֵי נִינְהוּ וְלָא מִיָּאֲשׁוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רבא's limit in step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They may be partners who own the coin jointly, and partners do not give up hope.

steps.title: Second version of רבא: even two פרוטות must be returned
steps.stepSummary: Another version of רבא's teaching says the finder must return the coin even if it is worth only two פרוטות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רבא said: Even if it is worth only two פרוטות, he is obligated to return it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second report of what רבא said. In this version, a coin worth only two פרוטות among three people must still be returned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two פרוטות split three ways is less than a פרוטה each. Under the first version of רבא, the finder could keep it. This version is stricter, and the next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (a second version of the teaching)

phrases.english: There are those who say: Rava said:
Even though it is not worth
more than two perutot,
he is obligated to return it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternative, stricter version of רבא's limit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the case of three, even a coin worth only two פרוטות must be returned.

steps.title: Reason: one partner may have given his share to another
steps.stepSummary: Perhaps they are partners and one gave up his share to another, leaving two partners with a פרוטה each.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Say they are partners, and one of them gave his share over to his fellow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second version of רבא. Maybe one partner gave his share to another, so only two partners own the coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one partner gave away his part, the coin now belongs to two people. Two פרוטות split between two is a פרוטה each, enough to require returning it. Even this possibility is enough to obligate the finder.
steps.whatToRemember: First version of רבא: three people must return the coin if it is worth a פרוטה each (three פרוטות). Second version: even two פרוטות, since one partner may have given his share to another.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Say that they are partners,
and one of them gave up
his share to his fellow.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא? אֵימוֹר שׁוּתָּפֵי נִינְהוּ וְחַד מִנַּיְיהוּ אַחוֹלֵי אַחֲלֵיהּ לִמְנָתֵיהּ גַּבֵּי חַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the second version of רבא in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One partner may have given his share to another, leaving two owners with a פרוטה each.

steps.title: Taking a lost coin before the owner gives up, planning to steal it
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that taking a fallen סלע before יאוש in order to steal it breaks לא תגזול, השב תשיבם and לא תוכל להתעלם. Returning it after יאוש does not undo the sin; it only counts as a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: someone saw a coin fall and took it before the owner gave up hope, meaning to steal it. He breaks all three commandments: 'Do not rob,' 'Return them,' and 'You may not ignore.' Even if he later gives it back after the owner gave up hope, that is just a gift. The sin he did stays done.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new teaching about which commandments a finder breaks. The first case is the worst one: grabbing the coin before יאוש with a plan to keep it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before יאוש the coin still fully belongs to the owner, so taking it to keep is real robbery. It also fails the duty to return it and the ban on ignoring it. Once יאוש comes, the coin legally becomes the thief's, so handing it back later is only a gift and does not erase what he did.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner giving up hope of getting his item back
'Do not rob': the ban on stealing
'You shall surely return them': the מצוה to return a lost item
'You may not ignore it': the ban on looking away from a lost item

steps.confusionAlert: Giving the coin back after יאוש does not 'fix' the sin. By then the coin legally belonged to the thief, so returning it is just a present.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the timing of יאוש decides who owns the coin. That is why a late return counts only as a gift.

phrases.english: And Rava says:
If one saw a sela coin that fell from someone,

phrases.aramaic: נְטָלָהּ לִפְנֵי יֵאוּשׁ עַל מְנָת לְגוֹזְלָהּ –
phrases.english: and took it before the owner's despair in order to steal it,
he violates all of them:
because of 'You shall not rob,'
and because of 'You shall surely return them,'
and because of 'You may not ignore it.'
And even if he returned it after the despair,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some have the one in square brackets. Both mean 'he returned it.'

phrases.english: it is a gift that he gives him,
and the transgression he did, he did.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching of רבא about which commandments a finder breaks.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking before יאוש to steal breaks all three commandments. A return after יאוש is only a gift.

steps.title: Taking it to return, then deciding to keep it after the owner gives up
steps.stepSummary: If he took it planning to return it and only after יאוש decided to keep it, he breaks only השב תשיבם.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he took it before the owner gave up hope, planning to return it, and after the owner gave up hope he decided to steal it, he breaks only 'Return them.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second, milder case. The finder started out honest and only later changed his mind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When he picked it up he meant to return it, so it was not robbery and he did not ignore the item. But he took on the duty to return it and never did, so he breaks only השב תשיבם.

phrases.aramaic: נְטָלָהּ לִפְנֵי יֵאוּשׁ עַל מְנָת לְהַחְזִירָהּ,
phrases.english: If he took it before the despair in order to return it,
and after the despair he intended to steal it,
he violates 'You shall surely return them.'

steps.triggerLanguage: נְטָלָהּ לִפְנֵי יֵאוּשׁ עַל מְנָת לְהַחְזִירָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's list with a milder case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Took it to return, then decided after יאוש to keep it: he breaks only השב תשיבם.

steps.title: Waiting until the owner gives up, then taking it
steps.stepSummary: If he waited until יאוש and then took the coin, he breaks only לא תוכל להתעלם.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he waited until the owners gave up hope and then took it, he breaks only 'You may not ignore it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his third case. The finder held back on purpose until the owner gave up, and only then picked up the coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After יאוש the coin is ownerless, so taking it is not robbery, and there is no longer a duty to return it. His only sin is that he looked away while he still could have returned it, which is לא תוכל להתעלם.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three cases. Took to steal before יאוש: all three commandments. Took to return, then decided to keep after יאוש: only השב תשיבם. Waited for יאוש, then took: only לא תוכל להתעלם.

phrases.aramaic: הִמְתִּין לָהּ עַד שֶׁנִּתְיָאֲשׁוּ הַבְּעָלִים וּנְטָלָהּ,
phrases.english: If he waited until the owners despaired and then took it,

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם ״לֹא תוּכַל לְהִתְעַלֵּם״ בִּלְבָד.
phrases.english: he violates only 'You may not ignore it,' alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבא's list with the third case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Waited for יאוש, then took it: he breaks only לא תוכל להתעלם.

steps.title: Coins that fall into sand need not be returned
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if someone sees coins fall from another person into the sand, then finds them and takes them, he does not have to return them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: someone sees coins fall from his friend into the sand, then finds them and takes them. He does not have to give them back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new ruling about one specific case: money that falls into sand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is surprising, because the finder actually saw whose money it was. The reason comes in the next steps.

phrases.english: Rava says:
This one who sees that coins fell
from his fellow into the sand,
and he found it and took it,
is not obligated to return it to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דְּחָזֵי דִּנְפוּל זוּזֵי מֵחַבְרֵיהּ בֵּי חָלָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching of רבא on a different case of יאוש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Coins that fall into sand belong to the finder.

steps.title: Asking the reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the finder may keep the coins.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבא's ruling. It is setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The finder knows exactly who dropped the money, so the ruling needs explaining.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why רבא's ruling in step 12 is true.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why may the finder keep coins he saw fall?

steps.title: The owner gives up hope
steps.stepSummary: Whoever drops money into sand gives up hope of finding it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The person the coins fell from has given up hope.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the owner has already given up on money lost in sand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Small coins in sand are almost impossible to find, so the owner gives up hope right away. Once there is יאוש, the money is ownerless and the finder may keep it.

phrases.english: That one from whom it fell
has given up hope.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner has יאוש on money lost in sand.

steps.title: Even sifting the sand does not show he still has hope
steps.stepSummary: Even if the owner is seen bringing a sifter and sifting the sand, he may only be hoping to find someone else's lost coins to make up his loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if the finder sees the owner bring a sifter and sift the sand, the owner is thinking: 'Just as my money fell here, other people's money fell here too, and I will find something.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא heads off an obvious objection: maybe sifting proves the owner has not given up. He answers that the sifting does not prove that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sifting could look like hope of finding his own coins. But the owner may have given up on his own money and only be searching for any coins other people dropped there. So the sifting is not proof against יאוש.
steps.confusionAlert: Searching does not always mean hoping for your own item. The owner may just be looking for any money that happens to be there.
steps.whatToRemember: Coins lost in sand are treated as given up by the owner, even if he is seen sifting for them.

phrases.english: Even though he sees him
that he brought a sifter and is sifting,
he is saying to himself:
Just as mine fell from me,
so too it fell from another person,
and I will find something.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל גַּב דְּחַזְיֵיהּ דְּאַיְיתִי אַרְבְּלָא וְקָא מְרַבֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the יאוש reason of step 14 against the evidence of sifting.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sifting the sand would show the owner has not given up.
steps.terutzMaskana: Sifting fits with יאוש, because he may just be hoping to find other people's coins.

steps.title: Finding items in a store or near a money changer
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that items found in the open part of a store, or in front of a money changer, belong to the finder. Items found behind the counter or between the chair and the money changer belong to the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone finds something in a store, he keeps it. If it is between the counter and the storekeeper, it belongs to the storekeeper. If he finds coins in front of a money changer, he keeps them. If they are between the money changer's chair and the money changer, they belong to the money changer.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sorts found items by where they were lying: the area customers use, or the private area behind the counter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Many people pass through a store, so the owner of a lost item gives up hope of getting it back, and the finder keeps it. The space behind the counter belongs only to the shopkeeper, so anything found there is assumed to be his. The same split applies to a שולחני.

keyTerms.meaning: A money changer, who works at a table

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
If one found items in a store, these are his.
Between the counter and the storekeeper, they belong to the storekeeper.
In front of a money changer, these are his.

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין הַכִּסֵּא וְלַשּׁוּלְחָנִי – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁל שׁוּלְחָנִי.
phrases.english: Between the chair and the money changer, these belong to the money changer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of coins lost in sand.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Items found in a public area of a store or before a money changer go to the finder. Items found in the owner's private space behind the counter or chair go to the owner.

steps.title: Coins found inside produce
steps.stepSummary: Loose coins found in produce someone bought or received belong to him. If the coins were tied up in a bundle, he must take them and announce that he found them.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone buys produce from his friend, or his friend sends him produce, and he finds coins in it, he keeps them. If the coins were tied together, he takes them and announces his find.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case: money hidden inside fruit or grain that someone received.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Loose coins have no identifying sign, so the owner can't prove they are his, and the finder keeps them. A bundle counts as a sign, so the finder must announce it and return it to whoever identifies it.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce, such as fruit or grain
Announces publicly that he found something

steps.whatToRemember: Location decides who owns a find in a store, and a bundle acts as an identifying sign that requires announcing.

phrases.english: One who buys produce from his friend,
or whose friend sent him produce,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָצָא בָּהֶן מָעוֹת – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ.
phrases.english: and he found coins in it, these are his.
If they were tied up, he takes them and announces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second section of the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Loose coins found in produce belong to the finder. Bundled coins must be announced.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: even coins on the table go to the finder
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר extends the משנה's money changer case. Even coins lying on top of the money changer's table belong to the finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: even if the coins are lying on the table itself, they belong to the finder.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רבי אלעזר explaining how far the משנה's ruling about coins found in front of a שולחני reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think the table belongs to the money changer, so coins on it are his. רבי אלעזר says no: even coins on the table go to the finder. The גמרא first tests this against the משנה's wording (steps 19-21). Then רבא explains where רבי אלעזר learned it (steps 23-24).

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who gives this ruling

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rabbi Elazar said:
Even if they are lying on top of the table.
phrases.notes: He is going back to the משנה's line about a money changer. Even then, the coins belong to the finder.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: אֲפִילּוּ מוּנָּחִין עַל גַּבֵּי שׁוּלְחָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how far the money changer clause of the משנה extends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Coins found on the money changer's table belong to the finder.

steps.title: The opening clause seems to contradict רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the משנה closely. It says 'in front of' the money changer, which suggests that coins on the table would belong to the money changer.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: in front of a money changer, the coins are the finder's. That implies that coins on the table belong to the money changer!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אלעזר using the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה chose the words 'in front of' the money changer. That seems to mean only coins in front of the table, not on it, go to the finder, which goes against רבי אלעזר.

phrases.english: We learned:
In front of a money changer, these are his.
That implies: on top of the table, they belong to the money changer!

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: לִפְנֵי שׁוּלְחָנִי – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי אלעזר's ruling from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's ruling that coins on the table go to the finder
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Inference from the narrow wording 'in front of the money changer': only coins in front of the table go to the finder, so coins on the table belong to the money changer.

steps.title: The closing clause implies the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers by looking at the end of the משנה. Only coins between the chair and the money changer belong to him, which implies that coins on the table go to the finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the last part: between the chair and the money changer, they are the money changer's. That implies that on the table, they are the finder's!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back by drawing an opposite inference from the end of the same line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If coins on the table belonged to the money changer, the משנה should have said so. Instead it gives him only the narrow space between his chair and himself. That suggests the table counts as the finder's area, which supports רבי אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: Say the last part of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: Both inferences come from the same line about the money changer. The opening part points one way and the closing part points the other way.

phrases.english: Say the last part:
Between the chair and the money changer, they belong to the money changer!
That implies: on top of the table, they are his.
phrases.notes: 'His' here means the finder's, not the money changer's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Cancels the challenge with an opposite inference from the end of the line.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The opening clause proves that coins on the table belong to the money changer.
steps.terutzMaskana: The closing clause implies the opposite, so the challenge is not decisive.

steps.title: Nothing can be proven from this משנה
steps.stepSummary: Since the two parts of the line imply opposite things, the משנה cannot settle the question of coins on the table.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, nothing can be learned from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the exchange. The משנה neither proves nor disproves רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each inference cancels the other, so the משנה simply does not address coins on the table. רבי אלעזר's ruling stands, since it was not contradicted.

keyTerms.meaning: Nothing can be learned from it

steps.whatToRemember: When the opening and closing parts of a משנה imply opposite things, the גמרא concludes that no inference can be drawn, and the ruling under discussion survives.

phrases.english: Rather, from this nothing can be learned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes that the two opposite inferences cancel out.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה gives no proof about coins on the table, so רבי אלעזר's ruling is not refuted.

steps.title: Where does רבי אלעזר get his ruling from?
steps.stepSummary: Since the משנה's wording points both ways, the גמרא asks what source רבי אלעזר relied on.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אלעזר, where does he learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא just said the משנה cannot decide the question of coins on the table. So now it asks how רבי אלעזר knew to rule that they belong to the finder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the plain wording of the משנה is unclear, רבי אלעזר must have had some other reason. The גמרא wants to know what that reason was.

keyTerms.meaning: Where does he get this from?
The אמורא who ruled that coins on the table belong to the finder

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar,
from where does he learn this?
phrases.notes: "This" is his ruling from step 18: coins lying on the money changer's table go to the finder.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from step 21's conclusion that the משנה's wording cannot settle the question, so a source is needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What source רבי אלעזר used for ruling that coins on the table belong to the finder.

steps.title: רבא: the משנה's narrow wording bothered רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that רבי אלעזר noticed the משנה chose an oddly narrow phrase, when it could have used a broader one like it did in its first part.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The משנה was hard for him. Why does it say specifically "between the chair and the money changer, they belong to the money changer"? It should have said "on the table," or "found in the money-changing place," the same way the first part says "found in a store, they are his."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question. רבי אלעזר did not read the משנה's words at face value. He asked why the משנה used such a narrow description.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If everything in the money changer's area belonged to him, the משנה could have said "on the table" or "in the money-changing place." That would match the first part of the משנה, which simply says "found in a store." Choosing the tiny space between the chair and the money changer must be on purpose, and step 24 spells out what it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה was difficult for him
Why specifically this? (Why choose this wording?)
Let it teach (it should have said)
The money changer's place of business
The first part of the משנה

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the משנה is wrong. "The משנה was difficult for him" means its wording raised a question, and the answer to that question is his source.

phrases.english: Rava said:
The mishna was difficult for him.
Why does it specifically teach
"between the chair and the money changer, they belong to the money changer"?
Let it teach "on the table,"
or else: "he found them in the money-changing place,"
as the first part teaches: "he found them in a store, they are his."
phrases.notes: Here "his" means the finder's. The first part of the משנה uses a broad place, "a store," with no small details.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 22's question by pointing to an unusual choice of words in the משנה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אלעזר learned his ruling from the משנה's choice of a narrow phrase over the broader phrases it could have used.

steps.title: So even coins on the table belong to the finder
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's narrow wording, רבא concludes that coins on the table belong to the finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn from it: even if the coins are lying on the table, they belong to the finder.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his answer. Because the משנה gave only the small space between the chair and the money changer to the money changer, coins on the table go to the finder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה could have used a broad phrase but didn't. That shows only the narrow area belongs to the money changer, and the table is left out. This is exactly רבי אלעזר's ruling, so his source is now clear.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי אלעזר's source is the משנה's careful wording. It chose the narrow "between the chair and the money changer" over a broad phrase like "on the table," so coins on the table belong to the finder.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a common way the גמרא reads a משנה. When it uses a narrow, specific phrase where a broader one was available, that choice is treated as teaching something.

phrases.english: Rather, learn from it:
even if they are lying on top of the table,
these belong to him.
phrases.notes: "Him" is the finder, not the money changer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from רבא's question about the משנה's wording in step 23.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Coins found on the money changer's table belong to the finder. רבי אלעזר learned this from the משנה's narrow wording.

steps.title: ריש לקיש begins to limit the produce-buyer ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה about someone who buys produce, and ריש לקיש, quoting רבי ינאי, begins to say the ruling applies only in a certain case.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: "One who buys produce from his friend..." ריש לקיש said in the name of רבי ינאי: They taught this only...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה, the case of coins found in bought produce (see step 17). It is setting up ריש לקיש's limit on that ruling, and his statement continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "They taught this only" tells us a limit is coming: the rule that the buyer keeps loose coins does not apply in every case. We will only find out which case it covers when the statement continues.

keyTerms.meaning: One who buys produce from his friend
Etc. (the rest of the quoted line)
They taught this only (a limit is coming)

phrases.english: "One who buys produce from his friend," etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה from step 17: loose coins found in the produce belong to the buyer.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יַנַּאי:
phrases.english: Reish Lakish said in the name of Rabbi Yannai:
They taught this only

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the money changer discussion and returns to the משנה's case of coins in bought produce.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש, quoting רבי ינאי, begins to limit the rule that a buyer keeps loose coins found in produce. The exact limit comes in the continuation.
